title: How would your architecture behave if one dependency became unavailable?
description: Learn to evaluate fault isolation, describe resilience patterns like circuit breakers and bulkheads, and explain how your system degrades gracefully when a dependency fails.

data.text: This follow-up checks whether you understand failure as a normal operating condition. A robust architecture does not assume dependencies are always available. Instead, it limits blast radius, fails fast, and keeps the most critical functionality alive.
Not all failures are equal. Start by separating synchronous dependencies from asynchronous ones, and critical paths from nice-to-have features.

rows: Replica failover, cached reads, queue writes

terms.definition: A pattern that stops sending requests to a failing dependency after a threshold is reached, giving it time to recover.
Isolating critical functionality into separate pools so one failing pool does not consume all resources.
A maximum wait time before a request is abandoned, preventing thread or connection exhaustion.
A degraded but safe alternative response when the primary path is unavailable.

data.title: Design for failure
data.text: Every external call is a potential outage. If a dependency has no timeout, no circuit breaker, and no fallback, a single slow response can cascade into a full system failure.

data.title: Payment gateway failure
data.content: Your checkout service calls a payment gateway synchronously. If the gateway times out, the checkout request fails. With a circuit breaker, after five consecutive failures the service stops calling the gateway for 30 seconds and returns a friendly 'payment unavailable' page instead of timing out every user.

data.title: Key takeaway
points: Assume every dependency will fail eventually
Use timeouts and circuit breakers to fail fast
Provide graceful degradation for the most critical user paths
